The Zambezi River. Southern Africa's most important river, the Zambezi flows approximately one thousand six hundred fifty miles from northwestern Zambia across eight nations to the Indian Ocean. It is renowned for the spectacular Victoria Falls and serves as the lifeline for agriculture, power generation, and transportation across the region.

The river creates Victoria Falls, one of the world's largest and most impressive waterfalls, forming the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. It flows eastward across southern Africa through Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Botswana before emptying into the Indian Ocean. The Kariba Dam, completed in nineteen fifty-nine, created Lake Kariba—the world's largest hydroelectric reservoir by volume—and provides power to multiple nations.

The Zambezi Basin covers roughly five hundred forty thousand square kilometers and is home to diverse ecosystems ranging from woodland to floodplain savanna. The river forms the boundary between Zambia and Zimbabwe for much of its middle course, a vital water source for both nations. Historically it served as a barrier to European exploration and colonial expansion in southern Africa. The river is subject to dramatic seasonal variation, and the flood season from November to April makes navigation hazardous in many sections.
